title: Hopf augmentation monomial basis and factorial convolution pairing
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. Let $C$ be a finitely generated commutative unital $k$-algebra with algebra maps $\Delta:C\to C\otimes_k C$, $\varepsilon:C\to k$ and a $k$-linear map $S:C\to C$. Assume $\Delta$ is coassociative with counit $\varepsilon$ and
$$m(S\otimes1)\Delta=m(1\otimes S)\Delta=\eta\varepsilon,$$
where $m$ and $\eta:k\to C$ are multiplication and unit. Thus these are the coordinate Hopf algebra axioms, with no cocommutativity assumption on $\Delta$. Put $I=\ker\varepsilon$. The vector space $I/I^2$ is finite-dimensional. Choose $x_1,\ldots,x_d\in I$ whose classes form a basis, allowing $d=0$, and let $v_i:C\to k$ be the linear functional with $v_i(1)=0$, $v_i(I^2)=0$, $v_i(x_j)=\delta_{ij}$, using $C=k\oplus I$. For linear functionals define convolution by $a*b=(a\otimes b)\Delta$. For $n\geq0$ with $n!\ne0$ in $k$, the classes
$$x^b=x_1^{b_1}\cdots x_d^{b_d},\qquad b\in\mathbf N^d,\quad |b|=n,$$
form a $k$-basis of $I^n/I^{n+1}$, where $I^0=C$. For $a\in\mathbf N^d$ put $V^a=v_1^{*a_1}*\cdots*v_d^{*a_d}$, with the empty product equal to $\varepsilon$. For $|a|=|b|=n$,
$$V^a(x^b)=\begin{cases}\prod_{i=1}^d a_i!&a=b,\\0&a\ne b.\end{cases}$$
Each $V^a$ annihilates $I^{|a|+1}$. For $d=0$, the degree-zero basis is $1$, and the degree-$n$ basis is empty for $n>0$.

source.place: Lemma 11.27, printed p.218, with the degree-n evaluation pairing from its proof; Sections 11e, 11.24--11.26, printed pp.216--218. The derivation iteration in the printed proof is interpreted after evaluation at the identity, not as an equality of global functions.

proof.text: Choose algebra generators $y_1,\ldots,y_s$ of $C$ and put $z_j=y_j-\varepsilon(y_j)1\in I$. They also generate $C$ as a $k$-algebra. Expand any polynomial in the $z_j$ into its constant, linear and degree-at-least-two terms. If its value is in $I$, its constant term is zero (apply $\varepsilon$), and its higher terms are in $I^2$. Thus the finitely many classes of $z_j$ span $I/I^2$, proving finite-dimensionality. The splitting $c=\varepsilon(c)1+(c-\varepsilon(c)1)$ and the dual coordinate maps of the chosen basis of $I/I^2$ give exactly the stated $v_i$. For $c=\alpha1+u$, $e=\beta1+w$ with $u,w\in I$, the term $uw\in I^2$ is killed, so $v_i(ce)=\alpha v_i(e)+\beta v_i(c)$. Hence each $v_i$ is a derivation at the counit.

source.place: Lemma 11.27, printed p.218; counit derivations as in 11.24, printed p.216. Product-rule details are supplied by the agent, with evaluation at the identity.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-convolution-linear-map-algebra] with $R=B=k$. The given coassociativity and counit identities are precisely its coalgebra hypotheses. It makes the full linear dual an associative convolution algebra with unit $\varepsilon$, so the ordered words $V^a$ and their empty-product convention are well defined. No interchange of adjacent $v_i$ is used.

source.place: Lemma 11.27, printed p.218; counit derivations as in 11.24, printed p.216. Product-rule details are supplied by the agent, with evaluation at the identity.

proof.text: For $r=|a|$, list $a_1$ copies of $v_1$, then $a_2$ copies of $v_2$, and so on. Apply [lem-sfb-bialgebra-counit-word-product-rule] to this list and $m=r+1$ elements $c_j\in I$. Every assignment of $r$ positions to $r+1$ factors leaves a factor empty; its contribution contains $W_\varnothing(c_j)=\varepsilon(c_j)=0$. Thus $V^a$ kills each such product, including $r=0$, where it is simply $\varepsilon$. An element of $I^{r+1}$ is a finite sum of these products: a coefficient in $C$ can be absorbed into one of the $I$ factors. Linearity proves $V^a(I^{r+1})=0$.

source.place: Lemma 11.27, printed p.218; counit derivations as in 11.24, printed p.216. Product-rule details are supplied by the agent, with evaluation at the identity.

proof.text: Let $n=|a|=|b|>0$ and write $x^b$ as a product of $n$ labelled factors, with $b_i$ copies of $x_i$. In the product rule of [lem-sfb-bialgebra-counit-word-product-rule], any non-bijection from the $n$ word positions to these $n$ factors leaves a factor empty and contributes zero. A bijection contributes the product of the numbers $v_i(x_j)=\delta_{ij}$. It contributes $1$ precisely when each position bearing $v_i$ is sent to a factor bearing $x_i$. There are no such bijections if $a\ne b$; if $a=b$, each of the $a_i$ positions may be bijected to its $a_i$ matching factors in $a_i!$ ways, independently for each $i$. Their number is $\prod_i a_i!$. This gives the displayed pairing without any commutation assertion for convolution.

source.place: Lemma 11.27, printed p.218; counit derivations as in 11.24, printed p.216. Product-rule details are supplied by the agent, with evaluation at the identity.

proof.text: For $n\geq1$, write each of $n$ factors in $I$ as $\sum_i\lambda_i x_i+q$ with $q\in I^2$, using the chosen quotient basis. Expanding their product, every term containing such a $q$ lies in $I^{n+1}$; the remaining terms are scalar multiples of the degree-$n$ monomials. Products of $n$ elements of $I$ span $I^n$ over $k$: absorb any ideal-multiplication coefficient into one factor. Thus the displayed monomials span $I^n/I^{n+1}$. If $\sum_{|b|=n}c_bx^b\in I^{n+1}$, Step 3 allows applying $V^a$ and Step 4 gives $c_a\prod_i a_i!=0$. Since each $a_i\leq n$ and $n!\ne0$, all factors $a_i!$ are nonzero in the field $k$, and their product is invertible. Hence every $c_a=0$, proving independence.

source.place: Lemma 11.27, printed p.218; counit derivations as in 11.24, printed p.216. Product-rule details are supplied by the agent, with evaluation at the identity.

proof.text: For $n=0$, the sole exponent vector is zero and its monomial is $1$. The splitting $C=k\oplus I$ identifies $C/I$ with $k$, so this is a basis; $V^0=\varepsilon$ evaluates it to $1$, the empty factorial product. If $d=0$, then $I/I^2=0$, so $I=I^2$ and $I^n=I^{n+1}$ for all $n\geq1$. Each positive-degree quotient is zero and the indicated empty family is its basis. The only word in that case is $V^0$, which kills $I$.
